A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same work and retain the same central estimation framework. Their complete main texts and appendices are readable, and visual inspection resolves extraction issues in equations, figures and tables.

before.justification: v1 reports original Monte Carlo results on estimation bias, confidence-interval coverage and calibration allocation in Section 5 and Appendix C.

after.justification: v2 reports Monte Carlo results, a distribution-shift simulation, and original Chatbot Arena evaluations using GPT-4.1-mini judgments in Sections 7–8 and Appendices D–E.

M1.justification: The estimator, confidence-interval formula and adaptive allocation rule are retained. Algorithm 1 corrects its final assignment from 'm1 ← m − m0' to 'm0 = m − m1', fixing the written budget-completion step. The printed estimator and confidence-interval code is unchanged.

E1.justification: v1 evaluates only synthetic binary-judgment simulations. v2 adds real human-preference data from Chatbot Arena, estimating win rates for six target models, and a distinct scenario where calibration and test label distributions differ while judge behavior remains fixed.

E2.justification: Beyond the retained naive-estimator and equal-allocation comparisons, v2 evaluates calibration-only, difference and conditional-calibration estimators against the proposed estimator in Figure 5. Table 1 identifies their formulas; the difference estimator is attributed to Angelopoulos et al. (2023a).

E3.justification: v2 adds an Arena protocol using GPT-4.1-mini, human-preference labels and random 90%/10% test/calibration splits. Its shift experiment fixes test accuracy at 0.5 and varies calibration accuracy from 0.25 to 0.75, with n=1000 and m=200. The n=200 simulation branch is removed. Both calibration budgets, 200 and 500, already existed in v1 and remain in v2.

E4.justification: Section 7 and Figure 5 add a substantive robustness analysis testing how calibration/test label shift affects competing estimators' bias. Conversely, v1's small-test-set sensitivity results in Appendix C.1–C.2 disappear. Analyses varying judge reliability and calibration budget remain.

E5.justification: v2 adds reporting over 100 random Arena splits, including averaged bias, interval coverage and interval length. The existing 10,000-replication Monte Carlo practice and 95% confidence-interval construction are retained; no increase in the retained simulations' replication count is stated.

E6.justification: v2 adds label-shift bias results and reduced Arena bias across all six targets. Table 2 reports 95%–99% coverage and average interval lengths of 0.178–0.267. Retained simulation plots also show different estimates and interval lengths under matching captions, while n=200 results disappear. The Figure 3 budget example changes from approximately 200 samples per class to 200 total despite retaining the same curves.

T1.justification: v2 adds Proposition 6.1 and its proof characterizing when calibrated LLM evaluation has lower variance than human-only evaluation. Section 7 formalizes label shift, confusion-matrix invariance and competing estimators' assumptions; Appendix B.3 adds an estimator-equivalence derivation. The earlier bias and allocation propositions remain, with the bias proposition reparameterized using total calibration budget.

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction and conclusion add two central contributions: identifying regimes where calibrated LLM evaluation has lower variance than fully human evaluation, and establishing robustness advantages over other estimators under calibration/test distribution shift. The original bias-correction, uncertainty and adaptive-allocation claims remain.

C2.justification: v2 explains the variance advantage over human evaluation and why label shift undermines competing estimators. It explicitly qualifies robustness through stable conditional judge behavior, discusses length/style dependence and multiclass estimation difficulties, and softens v1's assertion that calibration-label composition is fully controllable to something sampling strategies can sometimes influence.

D1.justification: v2 documents the Arena judge identity and response-pair construction, and Appendix D supplies the distribution-shift data-generation settings. The repository information and printed Python implementation are retained. Arena judge prompts and per-model sample counts are not supplied.

R1.justification: v2 adds a dedicated Related Work section and substantially develops positioning against prediction-powered inference and calibration-based estimation. New citations include PPI++, cross-prediction-powered inference, Kloos et al., Meertens et al. and Miller. Section 7 makes distributional assumptions a central distinction from prior approaches.

P1.justification: The abstract, introduction, problem setup and method/theory exposition undergo extensive rewriting, including contribution bullets and a more explicitly structured problem statement. Related work precedes the setup, empirical validation is divided into simulations and Arena evaluation, and Algorithm 1 moves to Appendix A. The appendix organization is substantially revised.

P2.justification: The main paper changes from one column to two columns, with redesigned figures, legends, captions and equation placement. v2 adds the human-variance diagram, distribution-shift plot, Arena bias chart and two tables. Eight small-test-set simulation figures are removed, and retained plots and the code listing are reformatted and redistributed.

improvement.justification: v1 supports the framework through stylized simulations. v2 substantially strengthens practical validation and method selection through Arena results, explicit estimator comparisons under label shift, and a proved variance comparison with human evaluation. These gains outweigh the removed n=200 simulations and the new Figure 3 budget-example error: the retained formula gives an interval length around 0.13 at 200 total samples, above the claimed 0.1 target. Missing Arena prompts and sample counts still limit reproducibility.
